newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Ringgit hits new 4-month high, seen rising.
newsitem.headline: Ringgit hits new 4-month high, seen rising.

text.p: The Malaysian ringgit reached a four-month high against the dollar on Wednesday and dealers and economists said it was likely to go higher.
The currency broke through the psychological barrier of 2.49 to the dollar, to stand 1.5 percent higher since the start of the week.

Dealers and economists told Reuters on Wednesday that ringgit buying remained largely speculative, with further gains seen in the next few days. "A lot of these (ringgit purchases) would be speculative," said Desmond Supple, regional economist with research firm I.D.E.A. in Singapore.
"While the direction of the ringgit's move has not caused much surprise, the extent of the upturn clearly has," he said.
Forecasts for the near term remained bullish.
"Dollar/ringgit has resumed the fall, heading for the 2.4840 July 1996 low after recent consolidation," I.D.E.A. said.
"At the current rate, a revisit of 2.4790, 1996's low, should come very soon," said research firm MMS International.
"These are actually position-taking by foreign investors for the new year," said a corporate dealer with a Malaysian bank.
He said the selling of long Singapore dollar positions against the ringgit had triggered the rally on Monday.

"Last year, people were expecting the dollar to go higher, probably 2.55. When it did not break 2.53, they probably thought the dollar will have a better potential to break higher if it drops first," the dealer said.
Most economists and dealers said the strength of the ringgit was due mainly to Malaysia's strong economic fundamentals and high interest rates.
"If you line up the economic fundamentals, they are favouring the ringgit's strength," said Sim Moh Siong, economist with Citibank in Singapore.
I.D.E.A. said the market's enthusiasm for the ringgit has also been fuelled by uncertainty surrounding the Thai baht and the Indonesian rupiah.

There has been speculation that central banks in Indonesia and Thailand will widen the band in which their currencies are allowed to trade relative to the dollar. This would weaken the currencies slightly and make them more attractive to investors.
Political uncertainties in the two countries have also affected their currencies.
"The inference is that once these factors become clear, the ringgit may cease to be the flavour of the month," I.D.E.A. said in a comment.

While the local stock market is looking forward to the additional liquidity generated by the ringgit's rise, the resulting inflow of funds has also begun pulling interest rates down, threatening Malaysia's tight monetary policy, the dealers and economists said.
"The strengthening ringgit should result in more investment-type funds coming into Malaysia, giving us extra liquidity," said a senior analyst at a foreign equities research house in Kuala Lumpur.
He said there would be a time lag before the Kuala Lumpur Stock Exchange's Composite Index started moving up.
Meanwhile, Malaysian interbank interest rates have fallen by around 15 basis points in the last three days.
"This could pose additional liquidity management problems to Bank Negara," said a foreign bank dealer in Kuala Lumpur.
The country's growing current account deficit and inflation had triggered worries about overheating last year and forced it to maintain a high interest rate regime and to slow growth.
Malaysia's 1996 gross domestic product growth is expected to fall to 8.2 percent, following 9.5 percent growth in 1995.
The country has reported nine straight years of growth over eight percent, which is expected to be maintained until the year 2000.
-- Kuala Lumpur newsroom (603-230 7509)
